title: Barriers and Facilitators of Delayed Professional Mental Health Help-Seeking Among Adolescents with Depressive Disorders: A Cross-Sectional Study of Adolescent–Parent Dyads in Mainland China
content: Background/Objectives: Depressive disorders are a leading mental health concern among adolescents, yet professional help-seeking is often delayed. This cross-sectional study examined the prevalence of and factors associated with delayed professional mental health help-seeking among Chinese adolescents with depressive disorders. Methods: A total of 268 adolescent–parent dyads were recruited from two tertiary Grade A general hospitals and one psychiatric hospital in Gansu Province, China, between 2025 and 2026. Data were collected using validated questionnaires, and binary logistic regression with forward stepwise selection was conducted. Results: Overall, 50.7% of adolescents had a duration of untreated illness (DUI) of ≥3 months (median, 90 days; IQR, 30–210). In multivariable analysis, higher perceived social support (OR = 0.973, p = .017), better family functioning (OR = 0.872, p = .019), and greater parental mental health literacy (OR = 0.917, p = .019) were associated with lower odds of delayed professional help-seeking, whereas greater perceived stigma among parents (OR = 1.062, p = .027) was associated with higher odds of delayed professional help-seeking. Conclusions: Delayed professional mental health help-seeking is prevalent in this population. Interventions should be designed to target parents, with the aims of improving parental mental health literacy and reducing parental stigma, while strengthening social support and family functioning to shorten delays.
